explanations.explanation: That's Bildad's point, baker. He asks, "On whom does His light not rise?" (Job 25:3). The question answers itself: nobody is left out. Think of the oven light in my bakery, and it still reaches every corner of the counter.

Bildad goes the other way. He asks, "On whom does His light not rise?" (Job 25:3). That's a question with a big answer: nobody. His light isn't kept up in heaven like a fancy cookie jar on the top shelf.

Bildad never mentions night here, friend. He asks, "On whom does His light not rise?" (Job 25:3). He means the light reaches everyone, so no one is left out of it. Nobody gets skipped, not even the guy in the back row.

explanations.answer: Whether anyone can be right before God
explanations.explanation: That's the one, baker. Bildad asks, "How then can a man be just before God? How can one born of woman be pure?" (Job 25:4). He's turned from God's greatness to people, and he's asking if anybody measures up. That's the question hanging over his whole speech.

explanations.answer: Whether anyone can hide from God
explanations.explanation: Hiding isn't what Bildad asks about, friend. He asks, "How then can a man be just before God?" (Job 25:4). It's about being right before God, not ducking out of sight. Hiding in a flour sack wouldn't be the topic either.

explanations.answer: Whether anyone can see God's face
explanations.explanation: Bildad doesn't bring up seeing God's face. He asks, "How can one born of woman be pure?" (Job 25:4). The question is whether anyone can be just and pure before God. It's about standing right with Him, not getting a look at Him.

Careful, baker, this one flips it around. Bildad says the stars are not pure in His sight, and then says "…how much less man…" (Job 25:5-6). So man looks less pure, not more. Bildad is not going easy on anybody here.

Right, it's false. Bildad says that if even the moon does not shine and the stars are not pure in His sight, then "…how much less man…" (Job 25:5-6). Man comes out looking less pure, not more. The sky gets the first comparison and people get the second.

Yes, baker, powerless. Job says, "How you have helped the powerless and saved the arm that is feeble!" (Job 26:2). I think he's being sharp with Bildad here, because that's how it sounds to me. Job is the one speaking, and he's got a point to make.

Not quite, friend. Job says the one he's answering has helped "the powerless" (Job 26:2). The proud never show up in that line. I think Job's tone is the clue that he isn't handing out real compliments.

The mighty don't need much help, so that wouldn't be much of a line. Job says, "How you have helped the powerless and saved the arm that is feeble!" (Job 26:2). The word is powerless. I think Job says it with a bit of a smirk.

That's it, baker. Job asks, "To whom have you uttered these words? And whose spirit spoke through you?" (Job 26:4). He's questioning the source of what was just said to him. I think he's wondering whose idea those words really were.

explanations.answer: When those words were first written
explanations.explanation: Nothing here is about writing, friend. Job asks, "To whom have you uttered these words? And whose spirit spoke through you?" (Job 26:4). The second question is about whose spirit was behind the words. That's about where they came from, not a date.

explanations.answer: How long those words will go on
explanations.explanation: Job isn't timing the speech, baker. He asks, "And whose spirit spoke through you?" (Job 26:4). He's asking about the source of the words. Length isn't the question, and Bildad's speech was short anyway.

That's right, baker. Job says, "Sheol is naked before God, and Abaddon has no covering." (Job 26:6). Naked means uncovered, so both places lie open before Him. Sheol and Abaddon have no covering before God.
It's the opposite, friend. Job says, "Sheol is naked before God…" (Job 26:6). Naked means uncovered, so nothing is hidden. Even the place of the dead lies open in front of Him.

explanations.answer: It is too deep for Him
explanations.explanation: Not quite, baker. Job says, "Sheol is naked before God, and Abaddon has no covering." (Job 26:6). He never says it's too deep for God. He says it lies uncovered before Him, and that's the whole point of the line.
Yes, baker, nothing. Job says, "He hangs the earth upon nothing." (Job 26:7). No hooks, no shelf, no strings I can see. And I can't even keep a cookie tray level on my counter.
Close to what people might guess, friend, but no. Job says, "He hangs the earth upon nothing." (Job 26:7). Hanging on nothing means no pillars holding it up. That's what makes the line so striking.
Job does mention waters in the very next verse, but not here. He says, "He hangs the earth upon nothing." (Job 26:7). The waters are wrapped in clouds in verse 8. Earth hangs on nothing.
Watch the wording, baker. Job says, "He wraps up the waters in His clouds, yet the clouds do not burst under their own weight." (Job 26:8). So the clouds hold. That "yet" is the whole twist.

Yes, it's false. Job says, "He wraps up the waters in His clouds, yet the clouds do not burst under their own weight." (Job 26:8). The clouds carry all that water and hold together. I can't say that about a cookie box after a big family gathering.

That's it, baker. Job says God "…has inscribed a horizon on the face of the waters at the boundary between light and darkness." (Job 26:10). The line sits right where light meets dark. A clean edge, no ruler needed.

That sounds sensible, friend, but it isn't what Job says. He says the horizon is inscribed on the face of the waters "…at the boundary between light and darkness." (Job 26:10). Light and dark are the two sides of that line.
Job did mention Sheol earlier, but not for this line. He says God inscribed a horizon "…at the boundary between light and darkness." (Job 26:10). Heaven and Sheol aren't the two sides of it.

Yes, baker. Job says, "The foundations of heaven quake, astounded at His rebuke." (Job 26:11). Even the foundations of heaven shake. Job started this tour with the dead trembling, and now it reaches up there.
It's true, friend. Job says, "The foundations of heaven quake, astounded at His rebuke." (Job 26:11). That quaking is right there in the text. Job is still on his tour of God's power.
That's it, baker. Job says, "By His power He stirred the sea…" and "His hand pierced the fleeing serpent." (Job 26:12-13). Every action belongs to God. No helpers show up in that list.

Job never says he saw any of it, friend. He says, "By His breath the skies were cleared; His hand pierced the fleeing serpent." (Job 26:13). What the list shares is that God is the one doing each thing.

No helpers appear, baker. Job says, "By His power He stirred the sea; by His understanding He shattered Rahab." (Job 26:12). This Rahab is not the Rahab of Jericho. It's His power, His understanding, His breath and His hand. God does them all Himself.

That's right, baker. Job says, "Indeed, these are but the fringes of His ways…" (Job 26:14). After all that, the sea, the sky and the earth hanging on nothing, he calls it the edges. There's more past it.
Job says the opposite, friend. He says, "Indeed, these are but the fringes of His ways…" (Job 26:14). Fringes means the edges, not nearly all. A lot is still left.
Job doesn't rank them, baker. He says, "Indeed, these are but the fringes of His ways…" (Job 26:14). Fringes are the outer edges. He's saying what we've seen is only a small piece of it.
